# 0009: Specific status codes, require Content-Length, never 503

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Modules:** upload-service, local
- **Source:** design doc, section "Status codes and Content-Length" (linked from README.md in this folder)

## Decision

Answer with specific codes and require Content-Length. Requiring a length lets the service stream with no buffering and
reject large files before reading them. Phones do not retry 429 and lose nothing: `app.log` carries its lines into the
next upload and the other files are full copies every time.

The codes: 400 for a bad name or a body that ends before Content-Length, 403 for a disabled type or an identity
problem, 408 for a body that stops arriving, 411 with no length, 413 when too large, 429 for the rate limit, a key
collision and storage failures. Tomcat sends the 400 and 408 for a broken body itself; the service records the same code
so the log line matches what the phone got.

## Rules for agents

Never return 503, and never read the body before every check has passed.

'413':
          description: |
            TOO_LARGE. Content-Length is above the type's `max-size` in `device-logs.file-types`,
            10 MB by default.
        '429':
          description: |
            The file may not have been stored. Phones don't retry on 429, and nothing is lost:
            app.log carries its lines into the next upload, and the other files are full copies
            every time. One of:

            - KEY_EXISTS: another file of this type from this phone was stored in the same
              millisecond. Nothing is overwritten, and the next upload gets a new receive time
              (ADR 0011).
            - STORAGE_FAILED: S3 failed the write or it ran past its 60 s deadline. Once the whole
              body was sent, S3 can still commit the object after the deadline. Never 503.
    head:

content.text:
**Why never 503:** Phones retry on 503 and on nothing else. They retry 3 times, 1 s apart, with the identical body, and ignore Retry-After. In the lab, a 503 sent after 100 Continue left `app.log` stuck for 300 s and held back the phone's other uploads. Those identical retries would also hit the create-only S3 key the first attempt may already have written, since S3 can still commit the object after the deadline. So a failed or timed-out write gets 429 (`STORAGE_FAILED`), never 503.

**Why 429 loses nothing:** Phones make one try on a 429 and don't retry. Nothing is lost because of what each upload contains:
- `app.log` holds only the lines added since the last successful upload, plus any lines whose upload failed. Lines from a rejected upload come back in the next one, and joining the stored pieces in order rebuilds the log.
- The `-now-` files and `calls.xml` are full copies every time, so the next upload replaces anything that was dropped.

The same reasoning is why the S3 client is built with `doNotRetry()`. The phone's body can be read only once, and a retry after a lost response would collide with the first write.
